title: When a key rotation fails to switch off the old key, should the gateway still tell the operator it rotated?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. When an operator re-keys a lost or stolen API credential and the step that switches off the old key fails, the gateway still answers 'rotated: true' while the old key keeps working. Our quality check read this in the code (gateway platform.ts lines 884 to 919) and measured it with a stand-in database, not a real one: the new key is saved, the old key stays active. I recommend telling the operator honestly that the old key is still live.

options.label: Refuse the rotation if the old key cannot be switched off
options.detail: The operator sees an error and nothing changes; safest, but a retry is needed.

options.label: Keep rotating, but answer 'rotated: false' and say why
options.detail: The new key still works; the operator is told the old key is live and must retry.

options.label: Leave it as is
options.detail: The operator keeps being told 'rotated: true' after a failed switch-off.

default_action: Option c: nothing changes. Wednesday leaves the ticket open and no agent builds it.

title: Which of six gateway sections that do not demand a login should be changed to require one?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. A check meant to confirm every /api section either requires login or is public on purpose was passing six sections that do neither: certifications, credentials, referrals, governance, nft and billing. Reading the code shows certifications and nft do turn away anonymous callers through other guards, and the other four go straight to the backend service; none was tested live. Changing this alters who can reach those sections, so it is your call. I recommend a read-only probe of what an anonymous request gets from each of the six before choosing.

options.label: Require login on all six now
options.detail: Anything public by design in those sections would break and need an exception list.

options.label: Probe the six on the shared test box first, then decide
options.detail: An agent sends one anonymous read to each section and reports the status codes; no change yet.

options.label: Record all six as public on purpose with a reason
options.detail: No behaviour change; the check turns green.

default_action: Option b's no-change half: nothing is re-gated and no probe runs until you answer. Wednesday asks the read-only agent to do the probe only after your tap.

title: Should the seven different 'who is a platform admin' lists be merged, and does the platform_admin role count?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. The gateway treats the role platform_admin as a super administrator in six places, but the key policy treats it as an ordinary user, and the sign-in service keeps seven more lists of its own. On 2026-10-20 you chose to keep it refused on certification reads and settle the rest in this clean-up. Only someone inserting that role by hand into the database can have it today. The seven-list count is from the ticket and was not recounted. I recommend one shared list without platform_admin, after a read-only check of who relies on it.

options.label: One shared list without platform_admin, after a check
options.detail: Tightest; changes who can do cross-tenant setup, so the check of who relies on it comes first.

options.label: One shared list that accepts platform_admin everywhere
options.detail: Consistent, but widens what a hand-inserted account can reach.

options.label: Leave the lists as they are for now
options.detail: The seven lists keep disagreeing; the 10-20 ruling stands.

default_action: Option c: nothing changes. Wednesday keeps the ticket parked and no agent edits a role list.

title: Should we fix the last case where a user's verification stays 'pending' while the screen says the request could not be confirmed?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. Most of this bug is fixed and live: a failed save now answers an error instead of 'ok'. One case was left alone on purpose: if the database connection fails twice in a row during an approval, the request ends up approved but the user's level is not raised, and the user sees an error (503). Nothing has been probed on the live system since the fix. I recommend leaving it, since the user is told it failed and can retry.

options.label: Build the fix for the double failure
options.detail: A new code change and review; stops the half-finished approval.

options.label: Accept it and close that part
options.detail: The user sees an error and an admin can re-approve; ticket closes after one live check.

options.label: Leave it open untouched
options.detail: The ticket keeps sitting open.

default_action: Option c: nothing changes and the ticket stays open. Wednesday does nothing further.

title: Accept the lower priority on the 'odd URL spelling skips the rate limit' problem and close it?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. The ticket worried that four odd spellings of an address would slip past the gateway's request limits. A test on a running stack showed three of the four are simply refused (404), and the fourth (a doubled slash) was already fixed and is live. Priority was lowered from highest to low on that basis, and the ticket asked for a second opinion because it is a security call. I did not test the MFA-disable route itself, because testing it would switch MFA off on an account. I recommend accepting and closing.

options.label: Accept low priority and close
options.detail: Relies on the login-route test and the doubled-slash fix being live.

options.label: Ask for one more test on a second limited route
options.detail: An agent repeats the test on a safe route; ticket stays open until then.

options.label: Keep the ticket open
options.detail: No change.

default_action: Option c: the ticket stays open with the lower priority. Wednesday does nothing further.

title: When the gateway turns a caller away for sending too many requests, should that refusal still be written to the audit log?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. Today every refused request still writes one audit entry (marked 429), and still costs a key check. A flood of refused requests is therefore a flood of database writes. The trade-off is a complete trail of who was refused versus load. The change would land in the audit middleware or in the gateway start-up order, and nothing was run live. I recommend keeping the audit entry and writing down why next to the limiter, with a test that pins it.

options.label: Keep auditing refusals; document and pin it
options.detail: No behaviour change; closes the open item as accepted.

options.label: Stop auditing rate-limit refusals
options.detail: Fewer writes, but a flood of refusals leaves no trace.

options.label: Sample or summarise refusals
options.detail: Some trail with lower load; a larger design change.

default_action: Option a is not applied without your tap: nothing changes and the item stays open. The Secuura agent on this ticket has stopped and writes no code.

title: Accept a known serious flaw in a database helper program until its maker releases a fix, or replace the helper?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. The database image carries one critical flaw (CVE-2025-68121) inside a small helper program called gosu, in the Go library it was built with. Newer database versions have the same flaw, so upgrading does not help. Nothing we run on the demo uses this image: the demo database is the managed Azure one, so exposure is on developer machines only (from the ticket's 2026-09 triage, not re-measured). The ticket has waited since 2026-09-08 for an upstream rebuild. I recommend accepting it until the rebuild.

options.label: Accept until the upstream rebuild; re-scan weekly
options.detail: No work; the weekly image watch tells us when it clears.

options.label: Replace gosu in our own image
options.detail: Works now, but we then maintain our own database image.

options.label: Leave the ticket blocked with no new check
options.detail: No change.

default_action: Option c: the ticket stays blocked and nothing changes. Wednesday takes no action.

title: Close the old CSS-tool vulnerability ticket on the source facts, or first read the running admin screen image once?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. A low-severity flaw in a build-time styling tool is fixed in the code on the main branch: all four lock files now pick the patched version and the audit no longer lists it. What is not shown is that the admin dashboard image running on the shared test box was built with it; that image was built 2026-10-06. The flaw only matters during our own build, never at run time. I recommend closing on the source facts.

options.label: Close on the source facts
options.detail: The running image is not read; risk is build-time only.

options.label: Read the running image once, then close
options.detail: One read-only look by an agent on the shared test box.

options.label: Keep open until the image is swapped
options.detail: Waits on a deploy that is itself waiting on you.

default_action: Option c: the ticket stays open. Wednesday does nothing until you answer.

title: Does the old 'flip tenant isolation to fail-closed' step still apply, or did later work replace it?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. This 2026 ticket described switching the database to refuse any read that does not name a tenant. Its trial change (pull request 191) was closed without merging, and its parent ticket KS-160 is marked Done. It was restored to In Progress in September only because it had been archived from that state. I have not compared it with the later tenant-isolation work (the ticket's reading of that is a hypothesis). I recommend one agent compares the two before any closing.

options.label: Close as replaced by KS-160 and the later work
options.detail: Fastest; relies on an unchecked reading.

options.label: Have an agent compare the two, then close or revive
options.detail: A read of the old plan against what shipped; no change until then.

options.label: Keep it open as is
options.detail: No change.

default_action: Option c: the ticket stays open untouched. Wednesday does nothing further.

title: When the admin audit log silently leaves out its platform half, should the response itself say so?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. If the platform part of the audit log cannot be read, the screen shows a normal-looking log with only the other half. A warning line now reaches our logs when the read throws an error (live in code), but the person looking at the page still cannot tell a short log from a log with a missing half. Adding a marker changes a published interface, so it needs a spec change and a review of its own. Ticket KS-1622 also asks whether such a window should drop the platform half entirely. I recommend adding the marker.

options.label: Add a marker to the response
options.detail: Callers and the admin screen can show 'partial'; an interface change with a gate.

options.label: Keep logs only
options.detail: Operators can see it in logs; viewers still cannot.

options.label: Add a marker later, after the audit screen is redesigned
options.detail: Parks it.

default_action: Option b is what stays in force: logs only, no interface change. Wednesday leaves the ticket open.

title: When a request for the proposals list misspells a filter, should it be refused, refused only when it looks like a typo, or ignored?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. The list of governance proposals ignores unknown filter names, so ?proposerid= or ?Status= quietly returns everyone's proposals instead of the filtered list. Upper-case status values are already refused and pinned with tests. Three more items stay open: control characters and no length limit on the proposer id (a 15 KB value was accepted). This is the item that changes the interface. I recommend refusing unknown filter names.

options.label: Refuse every unknown filter name
options.detail: Clear and simple; any client sending an extra key gets an error.

options.label: Refuse only near-misses of real filter names
options.detail: Fewer surprises, but a list of near-misses to maintain.

options.label: Keep ignoring unknown names
options.detail: Misspelled filters keep returning everything.

default_action: Option c: nothing changes. Wednesday leaves the ticket open and no agent builds it.

title: Close the 'active versus pending' starting value on the Microsoft 365 connections table as accepted?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. One of five definitions of the Microsoft 365 connections table starts new rows as 'active', outside the allowed values; the other four start them as 'pending'. The ticket says no code path can create a row that uses that start value. Whether any stored row has 'active' has never been read. I recommend closing it as accepted with the reasoning written beside the code.

options.label: Close as accepted
options.detail: Nothing can create such a row; reasoning is recorded.

options.label: Change the default to 'pending' to match the others
options.detail: A small change with a review.

options.label: Read the database for 'active' rows first
options.detail: One read-only check, then decide.

default_action: No change. The ticket stays open and Wednesday takes no action.

title: Delete the unused cache code in the shared services folder, or keep and repair it?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. The shared services folder now builds, but its cache section (15 files) is imported by nothing; only its types are used, by billing. The ticket has waited since 2026-09-14 for someone who knows the intent. Deleting dead code is safe if nobody means to use it. I recommend deleting the cache section and keeping the types.

options.label: Delete the cache section; keep the types
options.detail: Smaller code base; billing unaffected.

options.label: Keep and repair the cache section
options.detail: Only if something is meant to use it.

options.label: Leave as is
options.detail: The folder keeps carrying unused files.

default_action: Option c: nothing changes. Wednesday leaves the ticket In Review.

title: Which variable names should the load-test runner hide when it prints its command?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. The load-test tool prints the command it runs and hides values for a fixed set of secret-looking names. Names outside that set, and a web address with a username and password in it, still print in clear. No name the runner uses today is affected; nothing leaks now. I recommend hiding any name containing KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, PASSWD or CRED, and any address with credentials.

options.label: Widen the hidden names as recommended
options.detail: Small change in the runner; safer for future variables.

options.label: Keep the current fixed list
options.detail: The gap stays documented.

options.label: Hide every value
options.detail: Safest but makes the printed command hard to debug.

default_action: Option b: nothing changes. Wednesday leaves the ticket open.

title: Raise a test's 15-second time limit that runs out when the computer is busy?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. One load-test file has a 15-second limit; the work takes about 13.3 seconds when the computer is busy, and it timed out at 16.1 and 17.1 seconds on 2026-09-17. It is a test timing, not a product bug, severity Polish. An earlier fix attempt hit its round limit and shipped nothing. I recommend raising the limit to 30 seconds.

options.label: Raise the limit to 30 seconds
options.detail: Stops spurious failures; the test then takes longer to fail when really stuck.

options.label: Leave 15 seconds and rerun on failure
options.detail: The test keeps failing on busy machines.

options.label: Close the ticket; the time limit does not matter
options.detail: Accepts the flaky test.

default_action: Option b: nothing changes. Wednesday leaves the ticket open.

title: Try again on the test-helper fix that stopped at the review round limit, or close it?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. This ticket asks for three improvements to a test helper that reads configuration files. The first attempt (pull request 1278) was marked no-go at the round limit and shipped nothing. The ticket says that closing it is not the agent's call. The helper only affects our own tests. I recommend closing it, because none of the three gaps affects the product.

options.label: Close it
options.detail: No effort spent; the helper keeps its three known gaps.

options.detail: An agent redoes it and a gate reviews again.

options.label: Leave it open as is
options.detail: Sits on the board.

title: Try again on the fix for a security check that over-reports, or close the ticket?
bluf: Secuura/Blockchain. One of our code checks says a request body is inspected when a guard is defined but never called; the report is more optimistic than the code. The first fix (pull request 1268) was closed after one review round, because the reviewer found a defect in the walk logic. The ticket says it affects only our own check, not the product. I recommend retrying once.

options.detail: An agent redoes it under a gate.

options.label: Close it
options.detail: The check keeps over-reporting in that one shape.
